Future: Will, Going To, Present Continuous

You use different tenses in the future to express different events or situations.
You use will to talk about predictions and immediate decisions.
You use be going to to talk about intentions and plans.

Will is known as the predictive future, and describes known facts, or what we suppose is going to be true.
Example:
We will all become connected within the next five years.

Will is also used to express an immediate decision.
Example:
I'll buy the newest phone there is.

Be going to describes intentions or plans. At the moment of speaking the plans have already been made.
Example:
The next medium for communication is going to be an extension of consciousness.

Going to is also used to describe an event whose cause is present or evident.
Example:
Look at how fast new computers are! They're going to become the main communication instrument.
Decisions expressed with going to refer to a more distant point in the future.

The Present Continuous describes fixed arrangements, especially social and travel arrangements. A time reference is usually included.
Example:
Many people are attending an important lecture by Professor McLuhan this evening.
In the new electronic age, we will all become connected - part of a global village.
Information is going to move to every part of the globe at the same time.
The computer is going to be a communication and research instrument.
Many people are attending an important lecture by Professor McLuhan this evening.
Real Conditional: Expressing Truth Conditions
You use the Present Real Conditional to talk about true conditions in the present or in the future.
You use both If and When in the Present Real Conditional. When you want to talk about true conditions, If and When have the same meaning.

Example:
If you look it up, you find the term was coined by McLuhan.
When you read McLuhan, you read a voice describing the future we live in today.
Notice the structure of this type of conditional:
If/When ... Simple Present ..., ... Simple Present …

images.text: When you hear the term ‘global village’, what do you think of? If  you look it up, you find it was coined by Marshall McLuhan. Mr. McLuhan was a Canadian philosopher interested in media and how it would affect us. If you delve into his works, you find that his ideas were well ahead of their time. If you consider that his work was published long before the World Wide Web, it is quite astonishing. When you read McLuhan, you hear a voice describing a future we live in today. If you read on, some of his ideas are stated as I understand them.

It's the early '60s. Color television is not yet a household item. People still rely on their radios for musical entertainment. Music is recorded on vinyl. Payphones are available on the street if you need to contact someone while you are out. Answering machines are rare. Computers are huge boxes that fill a room and require data to be fed into them on cards. Enter Marshall McLuhan who thinks ...
  • The next medium for communication is going to be an extension of consciousness.
  • In the new electronic age, we will all become connected - part of a global village.
  • Information is going to move to every part of the globe at the same time.
  • The computer is going to be a communication and research instrument.
  • Advertisements are becoming the most truthful reflection of our society and its activities.
  • People are putting more thought into advertising as we move forward than in writing the actual features.

Today, ‘global village’ describes the Internet. On the web we cross distance in an instant, sending messages in real time. We are more involved globally. We are living proof that Mr. McLuhan's ideas were spot on.
